item.stem: Sodium and potassium are both group 1 elements. A student models the potassium compound analogous to Na₂O by replacing each Na⁺ ion with one K⁺ ion while leaving the O²⁻ ions unchanged. The model therefore contains two K⁺ ions for every O²⁻ ion. Is this model consistent with typical ionic bonding, and why?

choices.choice_text: Yes; potassium and sodium have the same typical ionic charge, so the replacement preserves electrical neutrality.
choices.rationale: Both elements have one valence electron and typically lose it to form ions with a +1 charge. Replacing Na⁺ with K⁺ preserves the charge balance: 2(+1) + (−2) = 0.

choices.choice_text: No; the subscript 2 in the analogous formula K₂O means that each potassium ion should be K²⁺.
choices.rationale: Subscript–charge confusion: a formula subscript counts ions; it does not specify their charge. Potassium typically forms K⁺, not K²⁺, because it has one valence electron to lose. Fix: Determine ionic charges from group position before interpreting formula subscripts.

choices.choice_text: No; potassium typically gains one electron to form K⁻, so the replacement produces only negatively charged ions.
choices.rationale: Electron-transfer direction reversal: group 1 potassium typically loses its single valence electron rather than gaining one. Losing an electron produces K⁺ because the ion has one more proton than electrons. Fix: Compare electron loss and gain to identify the nearest noble-gas configuration.

choices.choice_text: No; electrical neutrality requires equal numbers of potassium ions and oxide ions.
choices.rationale: Equal-count neutrality misconception: neutrality requires equal total positive and negative charge, not equal numbers of ions. One K⁺ and one O²⁻ would have a net charge of −1. Fix: Multiply each ion’s charge by its count, then add the charges.

item.stem: Fluorine and chlorine belong to group 17. To represent calcium chloride using a particle model of CaF₂, a student substitutes one Cl⁻ ion for each F⁻ ion and keeps the Ca²⁺ ions. The resulting representation has one Ca²⁺ ion for every two Cl⁻ ions. Does this representation agree with typical ionic bonding?

choices.choice_text: No; the subscript 2 in CaCl₂ requires each chloride ion to have a −2 charge.
choices.rationale: Subscript–charge confusion: the subscript counts chloride ions rather than specifying their charge. Chlorine typically gains one electron, forming Cl⁻ rather than Cl²⁻. Fix: Use the element’s group to determine ionic charge before interpreting subscripts.

choices.choice_text: No; chlorine typically loses one electron to form Cl⁺, making all the modeled ions positively charged.
choices.rationale: Electron-transfer direction reversal: chlorine typically gains one electron to complete its valence shell rather than losing one. Gaining that electron produces Cl⁻, not Cl⁺. Fix: Compare electron gain and loss to find the nearest noble-gas configuration.

choices.choice_text: Yes; fluorine and chlorine typically form ions with identical charges, so the substitution maintains electrical neutrality.
choices.rationale: Each element has seven valence electrons and typically gains one electron to form an ion with a −1 charge. Substituting Cl⁻ for F⁻ maintains charge balance: (+2) + 2(−1) = 0.

choices.choice_text: No; an electrically neutral model must contain equal numbers of calcium ions and chloride ions.
choices.rationale: Equal-count neutrality misconception: electrical neutrality depends on total charge, not equal ion counts. One Ca²⁺ ion paired with one Cl⁻ ion would have a net charge of +1. Fix: Multiply each ionic charge by its ion count and sum the charges.

item.stem: Aluminum is a Group 13 metal with three valence electrons. Which prediction best explains the formation of its typical monatomic ion?

choices.choice_text: Al³⁻ forms when an aluminum atom loses three valence electrons.
choices.rationale: Charge-sign reversal: Losing negatively charged electrons makes an atom more positive, not more negative. Losing three electrons produces a 3+ charge. Fix: Track how removing each negative electron changes the atom’s net charge.

choices.choice_text: Al³⁺ forms when an aluminum atom loses three valence electrons.
choices.rationale: Aluminum typically loses its three valence electrons to reach a noble-gas electron configuration. Removing three negatively charged electrons leaves the ion with a 3+ charge.

choices.choice_text: Al⁵⁻ forms when an aluminum atom gains five electrons.
choices.rationale: Wrong-direction octet trap: This reaches eight valence electrons but incorrectly predicts electron gain for aluminum. This metal typically loses its three valence electrons, exposing a filled inner shell. Fix: Identify whether the element is a metal before choosing electron loss or gain.

choices.choice_text: Al⁺ forms when an aluminum atom loses one valence electron.
choices.rationale: All-metals-are-1+ trap: Metals do not all form singly charged ions. Losing only one electron leaves aluminum with two electrons in its outer shell rather than a noble-gas configuration. Fix: Count how many valence electrons must be removed to expose a filled shell.

item.stem: A fireworks designer uses a strontium salt to produce a red flame. Strontium is a Group 2 metal with two valence electrons. Which statement best predicts the charge of the monatomic ion strontium forms in its salts and explains how that charge arises?

choices.choice_text: Sr²⁻ forms when a strontium atom loses its two valence electrons.
choices.rationale: Charge-sign reversal: the electron count is right, but the sign is backward. Removing negative electrons makes the atom more positive, so losing two gives 2+, not 2−. Fix: Track how each removed electron changes the net charge before writing the sign.

choices.choice_text: Sr²⁺ forms when a strontium atom loses its two valence electrons.
choices.rationale: As a Group 2 metal, strontium loses both valence electrons, leaving the noble-gas configuration of krypton. Removing two negatively charged electrons from a neutral atom leaves two more protons than electrons, so the ion carries a 2+ charge.

choices.choice_text: Sr⁶⁻ forms when a strontium atom gains six electrons.
choices.rationale: Wrong-direction octet trap: counting up to eight outer electrons seems to satisfy the octet, but metals lose electrons rather than gain them. Losing two electrons is far easier and exposes a filled inner shell. Fix: Ask whether the element is a metal before choosing electron loss or gain.

choices.choice_text: Sr⁺ forms when a strontium atom loses one valence electron.
choices.rationale: All-metals-are-1+ trap: metals do not all form singly charged ions. Losing only one electron leaves strontium with one valence electron, not a noble-gas configuration. Fix: Count how many valence electrons the group number gives, then remove all of them.

item.stem: Calcium belongs to Group 2 and has two valence electrons. As a neutral calcium atom becomes its usual monatomic ion in an ionic compound, which electron change and resulting charge are expected?

choices.choice_text: The atom releases two valence electrons and becomes Ca²⁻.
choices.rationale: Charge-sign reversal: Removing electrons increases an atom’s net positive charge rather than making it negative. Two electrons lost from neutral calcium therefore give a 2+ charge, not 2−. Fix: Determine the charge change caused by removing each negatively charged electron.

choices.choice_text: The atom accepts six electrons and becomes Ca⁶⁻.
choices.rationale: Wrong-direction octet trap: Adding six electrons would fill the outer shell, but this incorrectly predicts electron gain for calcium. This metal normally reaches a noble-gas configuration by shedding its two valence electrons. Fix: Use the element’s metal classification to choose electron loss or gain before counting electrons.

choices.choice_text: The atom releases one valence electron and becomes Ca⁺.
choices.rationale: All-metals-are-1+ trap: A metal’s usual ionic charge depends on its valence electrons, not simply its classification as a metal. Removing one electron leaves calcium with one outer-shell electron rather than a noble-gas configuration. Fix: Count the electrons that must leave before a filled inner shell becomes the outermost shell.

choices.choice_text: The atom releases two valence electrons and becomes Ca²⁺.
choices.rationale: Removing calcium’s two valence electrons exposes a filled inner shell with a noble-gas electron configuration. Because two negative charges are removed from a neutral atom, the resulting ion has a 2+ charge.

item.stem: Magnesium is in group 2, and nitrogen is in group 15. Which formula and ion-charge assignment correctly predict the binary ionic compound formed from these elements?

choices.choice_text: MgN, containing Mg²⁺ and N³⁻ ions
choices.rationale: The one-to-one ratio trap assumes that an ionic compound contains equal numbers of cations and anions. One Mg²⁺ and one N³⁻ give a net charge of −1, not zero. Fix: Add the ion charges for the proposed formula and check that the total is zero.

choices.choice_text: Mg₃N₂, containing Mg²⁺ and N³⁻ ions
choices.rationale: Magnesium typically loses two valence electrons, while nitrogen gains three to reach a noble-gas configuration. Three Mg²⁺ ions provide a total charge of +6, balancing the −6 from two N³⁻ ions.

choices.choice_text: Mg₂N₃, containing Mg²⁺ and N³⁻ ions
choices.rationale: The charge-as-own-subscript trap assigns each ion’s charge magnitude to its own subscript. Two Mg²⁺ and three N³⁻ give a net charge of +4 − 9 = −5. Fix: Find the smallest ion counts that make total positive and negative charges equal in magnitude.

choices.choice_text: MgN₂, containing Mg²⁺ and N⁻ ions
choices.rationale: The all-nonmetals-form-−1-ions trap gives nitrogen the wrong typical charge. Nitrogen has five valence electrons and gains three, not one, to reach a noble-gas configuration. Fix: Count how many electrons nitrogen needs to complete its valence shell before assigning its charge.

item.stem: A student is preparing a label for a binary ionic solid composed of aluminum (group 13) and sulfur (group 16). Which formula and typical ion charges belong on the label?

choices.choice_text: AlS, with Al³⁺ and S²⁻ ions
choices.rationale: The one-to-one ratio trap treats equal numbers of positive and negative ions as electrically neutral. One Al³⁺ paired with one S²⁻ has a net charge of +1. Fix: Calculate the total charge represented by the formula and verify that it equals zero.

choices.choice_text: Al₃S₂, with Al³⁺ and S²⁻ ions
choices.rationale: The charge-as-own-subscript trap uses each ion’s charge magnitude as that ion’s subscript. For Al₃S₂, the total charge is +9 − 4 = +5, so the formula is not neutral. Fix: Determine the smallest ion counts that balance total positive and negative charges.

choices.choice_text: Al₂S₃, with Al³⁺ and S²⁻ ions
choices.rationale: Aluminum loses three valence electrons and sulfur gains two to attain noble-gas configurations. Two Al³⁺ ions contribute +6, while three S²⁻ ions contribute −6, making Al₂S₃ electrically neutral.

choices.choice_text: AlS₃, with Al³⁺ and S⁻ ions
choices.rationale: The all-nonmetals-form-−1-ions trap incorrectly assigns sulfur a −1 charge. Sulfur has six valence electrons, so completing its valence shell requires gaining two electrons rather than one. Fix: Count the electrons sulfur must gain to complete its valence shell before assigning its charge.
